rationale: The student added both numerators and denominators (2/5 + 1/5 = 3/10). A number-line addition model partitioned into fifths demonstrates that jumping forward adds more fifths along the same scale, so the denominator stays 5 rather than becoming tenths.

script.focus: The denominator stays fifths because hopping adds more fifth-sized parts along the line.

intent: Demonstrate add on the number-line with values [1,3] (unit 1/5). Tutor points at: The denominator stays fifths because hopping adds more fifth-sized parts along the line.

frames.caption: Start at 1/5. We are standing here; we have not hopped yet.
Hop 1 moves 1/5 forward and lands on 2/5. One hop is one fifth.
Hop 3 lands on 4/5. 3 hops, so 1/5 + 3/5 = 4/5. Every hop was one fifth; the size of the pieces never changed, only how many.

judgement.reasoning: The student adds both denominators (getting 3/10 for 2/5 + 1/5). The demo switches representation from a fraction bar to a number line hopping in fifths, explicitly demonstrating 1/5 + 3/5 = 4/5 and emphasizing that hop size remains fifths throughout. It is ungraded, prerequisite/simpler worked example that directly addresses the misconception.
judgement.verdict: Yes, a teacher would use this worked demonstration because it provides a visual number-line model reinforcing why fifths stay fifths without spoiling the original problem.
